newsitem.title: BELGIUM: ROBECO GROUP STARTS EMU-CURRENCIES SAVINGS ACCOUNT.
newsitem.headline: ROBECO GROUP STARTS EMU-CURRENCIES SAVINGS ACCOUNT.

text.p: Dutch fund management group Robeco launched on Monday what it said was the first multi-currency savings account designed with European economic and monetary union (EMU) in mind.

EuRoparco will offer the same interest rate to savers whether they invest in Dutch guilders, Deutsche marks, Belgian or Luxembourg francs, or French francs, Guido van Berkel, managing director of Roparco NV, which will manage EuRoparco, told a news conference.
"It is our strong belief EMU will happen in 1999 and these currencies will participate," van Berkel said.
"By launching EuRoparco, the Robeco Group anticipates that move by allowing European savers to get acquainted with the financial environment of the near future," van Berkel added.
The account will be marketed by Robeco Bank Luxembourg SA, where account holders must have a minimum balance of one million Luxembourg francs, or equivalent.

EuRoparco is based on the Roparco savings account launched in the Netherlands 15 years ago and which now claims five percent of the Dutch savings market, with assets under management of around 12 billion guilders (240 billion Belgian francs), van Berkel said.
Roparco, although regulated as a bank, acts like a fund investing in deposits, bonds, mortgages and other instruments, van Berkel said.
It was too early to say what proportion of assets might now be invested in EuRoparco account currencies.

"I have not taken investment decisions yet to prepare for potential flows in Belgian francs, marks or French francs because that would deliver too much of an exchange rate risk, which as a bank we are not allowed," he said.
He said, however, the multi-currency account had been welcomed by both the Dutch central bank and Luxembourg's regulatory Institut Monetaire Luxembourgeois.

Robeco said EuRoparco would start by offering an annual interest rate of 4.10 percent compared to money market rates in the Netherlands, Germany, France, Belgium and Luxembourg of under or around 3.00 percent and lower still domestic bank deposit savings account rates.

Van Berkel said there were no plans to extend the account to investors holding Italian lira, Danish krona or Spanish pesetas because convergence of their bond markets ahead of EMU was not at such an advanced stage.
